title: 2 Samuel 13:23–39
context: Two years later, Absalom invites the king’s sons to a sheep-shearing feast and has his servants kill Amnon. A false report that all the king’s sons are dead throws David into grief until Jonadab, who knew of Absalom’s intent, explains that only Amnon has died. Absalom flees to his grandfather in Geshur for three years, and David eventually longs for him. Absalom’s revenge is neither justice nor righteous vengeance. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about the spreading consequences of unaddressed sin.

verses.text: After two full years, Absalom had sheep shearers in Baal Hazor, which is beside Ephraim; and Absalom invited all the king’s sons.
verses.arminianNotes:
Two full years later, Absalom holds a sheep-shearing festival at Baal Hazor and invites all the king’s sons. His plan is patient.

Arminian readers see long-held hatred moving toward action.
verses.reformedNotes:
The two years show that Absalom’s anger has hardened into a settled plan. Sheep shearing could be an occasion for feasting (compare 1 Samuel 25:2, 36).

Reformed readers see sin maturing in the heart. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the delay of justice under David has left room for private revenge.

verses.text: Absalom came to the king and said, “See now, your servant has sheep shearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom invites the king and his servants to the shearing. The invitation seems generous.

Arminian readers see deception in Absalom’s apparent hospitality. The invitation to the king is part of a hidden plan, which the narrator will soon make clear.
verses.reformedNotes:
The request is outwardly respectful. Absalom’s intent is hidden.

Reformed readers see concealment preparing for violence. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the echo of Amnon’s earlier use of the king’s goodwill to reach his goal.

verses.text: The king said to Absalom, “No, my son, let’s not all go, lest we be burdensome to you.” He pressed him; however he would not go, but blessed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
David declines, not wanting to be a burden, but blesses Absalom. The king suspects nothing.

Arminian readers see David again unaware of what is happening in his family, as he was with Amnon.
verses.reformedNotes:
David’s refusal is courteous. His blessing is sincere.

Reformed readers see the king’s blindness to his sons’ hearts. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting a pattern in which David is used by his sons’ schemes, as in verse 7.

verses.text: Then Absalom said, “If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us.” The king said to him, “Why should he go with you?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom asks that Amnon at least go with them; David asks why he should go. The request raises a question.

Arminian readers see David’s hesitation, perhaps a faint suspicion that he does not pursue.
verses.reformedNotes:
David’s question hints at unease. He does not press it.

Reformed readers see an opportunity for discernment that passes. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without speculating beyond the narrator’s brief report of the king’s question.

verses.text: But Absalom pressed him, and he let Amnon and all the king’s sons go with him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom presses, and David lets Amnon and all the king’s sons go. The plan proceeds.

Arminian readers see David yielding to persistent pressure, with tragic results. Once again his son’s request leads to harm.
verses.reformedNotes:
The king consents. His decision opens the way for Absalom’s revenge.

Reformed readers see events moving toward the judgment foretold in 12:10. Both traditions read this as shared ground, holding David’s choices, Absalom’s intent, and God’s word of judgment together without explaining away any of them.

verses.text: Absalom commanded his servants, saying, “Mark now, when Amnon’s heart is merry with wine; and when I tell you, ‘Strike Amnon,’ then kill him. Don’t be afraid. Haven’t I commanded you? Be courageous, and be valiant!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom orders his servants to kill Amnon when he is merry with wine, assuring them, “Haven’t I commanded you?” He takes the place of judge.

Arminian readers see murder planned and commanded, not justice done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Absalom acts as avenger outside any lawful process. He relieves his servants of fear by claiming authority.

Reformed readers see private vengeance usurping God’s justice. Both traditions read this as shared ground: Absalom’s revenge is neither justice nor righteous vengeance.

verses.text: The servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king’s sons arose, and every man got up on his mule and fled.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom’s servants kill Amnon as commanded, and the king’s sons flee on their mules. Violence breaks out at the feast.

Arminian readers see sin bearing deadly fruit in David’s house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Amnon dies by his brother’s command. The narrator reports it briefly.

Reformed readers see the sword not departing from David’s house (12:10). Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground, mourning the violence without treating it as righteous judgment.

verses.text: While they were on the way, the news came to David, saying, “Absalom has slain all the king’s sons, and there is not one of them left!”
verses.arminianNotes:
A report reaches David that Absalom has killed all the king’s sons. The rumor is worse than the truth.

Arminian readers see fear and confusion spreading in the wake of violence.
verses.reformedNotes:
The exaggerated report heightens the crisis. David’s worst fear seems realized.

Reformed readers see the turmoil sin brings to a household and kingdom. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the truth will soon be clarified by Jonadab.

verses.text: Then the king arose, and tore his garments, and lay on the earth; and all his servants stood by with their clothes torn.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king tears his garments and lies on the ground, and his servants stand by with torn clothes. Grief is immediate.

Arminian readers see sincere sorrow, though it comes after justice was neglected.
verses.reformedNotes:
David mourns deeply. His grief is genuine.

Reformed readers see the bitter consequences of sin in his house. Both traditions read this as shared ground, recognizing both David’s real grief and his earlier failure to act on Tamar’s behalf in verse 21.

verses.text: Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David’s brother, answered, “Don’t let my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men, the king’s sons, for Amnon only is dead; for by the appointment of Absalom this has been determined from the day that he forced his sister Tamar.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonadab tells David that only Amnon is dead, and that Absalom had determined this since the day Amnon forced Tamar. He knew.

Arminian readers see Jonadab’s knowledge revealing his complicity and silence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonadab, who devised Amnon’s scheme, now interprets Absalom’s. He seems to have foreseen it.

Reformed readers see a counselor who enabled sin and then watched it unfold. Both traditions name his role plainly and read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Now therefore don’t let my lord the king take the thing to his heart, to think that all the king’s sons are dead; for only Amnon is dead.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonadab tells the king not to take it to heart, for only Amnon is dead. His words minimize the loss.

Arminian readers see a callousness that matches his earlier counsel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonadab’s reassurance is cold. Amnon’s death is still a grievous loss to David.

Reformed readers see how shallow counsel treats sin and grief lightly. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without commending Jonadab’s words as comfort.

verses.text: But Absalom fled. The young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming by way of the hillside behind him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom flees, and the watchman sees many people coming along the hillside. The narrative alternates between flight and return.

Arminian readers see Absalom choosing exile rather than facing the consequences.
verses.reformedNotes:
Absalom’s flight confirms his guilt. The approaching crowd brings news.

Reformed readers see the scene moving toward the king’s sons’ arrival. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, noting the narrator’s careful pacing in a moment of crisis.

verses.text: Jonadab said to the king, “Behold, the king’s sons are coming! It is as your servant said.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonadab tells the king that his sons are coming, as he said. He claims to have been right.

Arminian readers see Jonadab more concerned with being right than with the harm he helped cause.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonadab’s words emphasize his own accuracy. His role in the tragedy is unacknowledged.

Reformed readers see self-interest in his speech. Both traditions read this as shared ground and name his complicity plainly, without treating his foresight as a virtue.

verses.text: As soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the king’s sons came, and lifted up their voices and wept. The king also and all his servants wept bitterly.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king’s sons arrive weeping, and the king and his servants weep bitterly. The household mourns together.

Arminian readers see genuine grief at the consequences of sin within the family.
verses.reformedNotes:
The weeping is shared and bitter. The loss is real.

Reformed readers see the sorrow foretold in 12:10–12 unfolding. Both traditions read this as shared ground and with compassion, recognizing that sin brings grief to many beyond those who commit it.

verses.text: But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihur, king of Geshur. David mourned for his son every day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom flees to Talmai son of Ammihur, king of Geshur, and David mourns for his son every day. Talmai was Absalom’s maternal grandfather (2 Samuel 3:3).

Arminian readers see Absalom seeking refuge with family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Absalom finds safety outside Israel. David’s daily mourning is noted.

Reformed readers see the family fractured by sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground; the text does not specify whether David mourns for Amnon or Absalom here, and these notes do not settle it.

verses.text: So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom stays in Geshur for three years. His exile is long.

Arminian readers see the cost of his choices: separation from his father and his homeland. Murder has not brought him peace.
verses.reformedNotes:
The three years of exile mark a lasting break. No resolution is offered.

Reformed readers see sin’s consequences continuing over time. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that neither justice nor reconciliation has yet been pursued, which sets the stage for chapter 14.

verses.text: King David longed to go out to Absalom, for he was comforted concerning Amnon, since he was dead.
verses.arminianNotes:
King David longs to go out to Absalom, having been comforted concerning Amnon. His feelings shift.

Arminian readers see a father’s love persisting despite his son’s crime. Love without justice, however, leaves the wrong unresolved.
verses.reformedNotes:
David’s longing for Absalom sets up Joab’s plan in chapter 14. The text does not resolve the tension between love and justice.

Reformed readers see grief, love, and unresolved wrong mixed together. Both traditions read this as shared ground and decline to excuse either the murder or the king’s inaction.
